Lesson Overview

Last time, you explored how to classify the different parts of your mousetrap car based on their end-of-life potential — whether a component could be reused, recycled, or would become waste. That was an important step in recognizing your responsibility as an engineer.

Today, you are diving deeper into a crucial phase of the Creationeering process: Death & Recycling. Specifically, you will focus on a growing challenge in our modern world — E-Waste — and how to safely dispose of materials, even those from your seemingly simple mousetrap car. Every material you choose and every design decision you make has consequences for its entire lifespan, right up to its very end.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Define E-Waste and identify common hazardous materials found in electronic devices.
  • Explain the environmental and health impacts of improper waste disposal, particularly E-Waste.
  • Identify materials in your mousetrap car that might require special consideration for disposal or recycling.
  • Propose methods for responsibly disposing of or recycling components from your mousetrap car.
  • Connect responsible waste management to biblical stewardship and God's call to care for His creation.

data.html:
Stewards of the Earth's Endings

As engineers, it is easy to get excited about the beginning of a project — the brainstorming, the building, the testing. But great engineers also think about the end. What happens to your design when it is no longer useful? What happens to the materials that made it?

This is exactly what the Creationeering phase of Death & Recycling asks you to consider. It is not a morbid topic — it is actually one of the most responsible things you can do as a designer. God built cycles of renewal into creation itself: seasons change, leaves fall and decompose, nutrients return to the soil. Engineers who think about end-of-life are following that same pattern of purposeful design.

Psalm 24:1 — "The earth is the Lord's, and everything in it, the world, and all who live in it."

You are not the owner of the materials you build with. You are a caretaker. That changes how you think about every design decision, including what happens at the very end of your product's life.

What Is E-Waste?

E-Waste — short for electronic waste — is any discarded device or component that runs on electricity or contains electronic parts. Old phones, broken laptops, dead batteries, worn-out circuit boards: all of these are E-Waste. And there is a lot of it. Globally, tens of millions of metric tons of E-Waste are generated every single year, making it one of the fastest-growing waste streams on the planet.

Here is what makes E-Waste especially tricky: many electronic components contain hazardous materials — substances like lead, mercury, cadmium, and arsenic. These materials are incredibly useful inside a working device. But when a device ends up in a landfill and begins to break down, those same materials can leach into the soil and groundwater, poisoning ecosystems and harming human health.

Think of it like a well-designed machine that works perfectly in normal conditions but causes serious damage when it fails in the wrong environment. The problem is not the material itself — it is where it ends up.

data.caption: A pile of discarded electronics including old phones, circuit boards, and batteries, illustrating the scale of the global E-Waste problem

data.html:
Why Improper Disposal Is a Big Deal

When E-Waste is thrown into a regular trash bin, it often ends up in a landfill. Landfills are designed to contain waste, but they are not perfect barriers. Over time, hazardous materials can escape. Here is what improper E-Waste disposal can cause:

  • Soil contamination — toxic metals absorb into the ground, killing plants and entering the food chain.
  • Water pollution — chemicals leach into groundwater and nearby rivers, harming aquatic life and making water unsafe to drink.
  • Air pollution — when E-Waste is burned (a common practice in some regions), toxic fumes are released into the atmosphere.
  • Health risks — communities near improperly managed E-Waste sites experience higher rates of illness, particularly in children.

These are not abstract statistics. These are real consequences that fall disproportionately on vulnerable communities around the world. Being a responsible engineer means caring about those consequences — even when they happen far from your workbench.

Your Mousetrap Car and End-of-Life Thinking

Your mousetrap car might not look like a smartphone or a laptop. But look closer. Your build likely includes materials like wood, metal axles, rubber bands, plastic wheels, and possibly a metal spring mechanism. Some of these are easy to deal with responsibly. Others need more careful thought.

Materials to Consider

  • Wood and cardboard — biodegradable and compostable. These decompose naturally without releasing harmful substances.
  • Metal components (axles, screws, the mousetrap spring) — highly recyclable. Most scrap metal can be melted down and reformed into new products endlessly.
  • Rubber (bands, tires) — harder to recycle but not hazardous. Some facilities accept rubber for repurposing.
  • Plastic wheels or connectors — recyclability depends on the plastic type. Check the recycling symbol and number on the plastic if available.
  • Adhesives and paints — some contain chemicals that classify them as hazardous waste. Do not pour them down the drain or throw them in regular trash.

The mousetrap car is a small-scale model of a much bigger engineering reality. Every product ever made — from a toy car to a commercial aircraft — has to be designed with its eventual retirement in mind.

data.caption: A labeled diagram of a mousetrap car with arrows pointing to each material component and its recommended end-of-life disposal category: compost, recycle, or special disposal

data.html:
Safe Disposal Methods

Knowing that certain materials need special handling is only useful if you also know what to actually do with them. Here are the main pathways for responsible disposal:

Certified E-Waste Recyclers

Many cities and counties have certified E-Waste collection events or drop-off locations. These facilities are equipped to safely dismantle electronics, recover valuable materials like gold and copper, and properly contain hazardous substances. Look for certifications like e-Stewards or R2 — these indicate that a recycler meets rigorous environmental and safety standards.

Manufacturer Take-Back Programs

Many electronics companies — Apple, Dell, Best Buy, and others — offer programs where you can return old devices for responsible recycling. Some even offer store credit. This is called a take-back program, and it is one of the easiest ways for consumers to dispose of electronics responsibly.

Donation and Refurbishment

If a device still works, the most sustainable option is to extend its life. Donating functioning electronics to schools, nonprofits, or community organizations keeps them out of the waste stream entirely. Obsolescence does not always mean broken — sometimes it just means newer models are available. A working device that gets a second life is always better than one that goes straight to recycling.

Household Hazardous Waste (HHW) Programs

For items like batteries, paint, and certain adhesives from your mousetrap car builds, your local government may operate a Household Hazardous Waste program. These programs accept materials that cannot go in regular trash and ensure they are processed safely.

Before your mousetrap car project wraps up, take five minutes to write out a simple End-of-Life Plan for your build. List each material, identify its category (compostable, recyclable, hazardous), and note where you would take it for proper disposal. This is exactly the kind of thinking professional engineers document in a full product lifecycle assessment.

Multiscale Thinking: From Your Car to the Planet

Here is where multiscale modeling becomes a powerful concept. When you look at your mousetrap car, you can think about it at multiple scales:

  • Macro scale — the whole car: how does it move, how does it perform, what does it look like?
  • Material scale — the individual components: what are they made of, how durable are they, how will they behave over time?
  • Molecular scale — what happens to these materials as they age, decompose, or interact with other substances in a landfill?

This kind of layered thinking is exactly what environmental engineers and materials scientists use when designing products for sustainability. A decision that seems small at the macro scale — like choosing one type of plastic over another — can have enormous consequences at the molecular scale, affecting how long a material persists in the environment and what it releases as it breaks down.

God designed creation to work across scales too. The tiny water cycle operating at the molecular level feeds the massive global weather systems we experience every day. As engineers made in His image, we are invited to think with that same depth.

Design with the End in Mind

The best engineers do not just ask, "Will this work?" They also ask, "What happens when this stops working?" That second question is harder to answer, but it is just as important. It requires you to think ahead — sometimes years or decades into the future — and consider impacts that you may never personally witness.

Genesis 1:28 calls humanity to rule over creation — but this is a steward's rule, not an exploiter's rule. It is the kind of leadership that leaves things better than it found them. When you design your mousetrap car with its end-of-life in mind, you are practicing exactly that kind of leadership. Small scale today. World-changing mindset for tomorrow.

Common Mistake: Many students assume that because their mousetrap car is simple or small, its end-of-life does not matter. Do not fall into that trap. The habits you build now — thinking about material choices, disposal pathways, and environmental impact — are the same habits that professional engineers apply to billion-dollar products. Start practicing them at every scale.

data.title: Going Deeper: The Global E-Waste Crisis
data.html:
The scale of the global E-Waste problem is staggering. According to the Global E-Waste Monitor, the world generated over 53 million metric tons of E-Waste in a single recent year — and less than 20% of it was formally recycled. The rest ended up in landfills, was illegally exported to developing nations, or was processed in informal recycling operations with no safety standards.

Informal E-Waste processing — where workers, sometimes including children, manually dismantle electronics without protective equipment — is a serious human rights and environmental justice issue. Toxic exposure in these communities causes long-term neurological damage, respiratory illness, and elevated cancer rates.

Some countries are beginning to address this through Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) laws, which require manufacturers to take responsibility for the end-of-life of their products. This is essentially legislating the stewardship principle into business practice. As a future engineer or entrepreneur, you may one day design products that fall under these regulations — or you may advocate for stronger ones.
